title: Canada stops using 'avalanche dogs' for rescues in Rocky Mountains, stirring outrage
description: Scott Ward can still recall the relief he saw on parents' faces when a search and rescue dog he was working with found their children safe in Canada's
body: Scott Ward can still recall the relief he saw on parents' faces when a search and rescue dog he was working with found their children safe in Canada's vast and heavily wooded Banff National Park.Another time, his canine partner led him hiking up a steep mountainside for two hours until they reached a man with a broken leg who was close to dying from hypothermia.Now 73 and retired, Ward spent 17 years as a dog handler in the wilderness of the Canadian Rocky Mountains, work he described as gratifying.Over the years, the rescue programme was cut back to just one person in the role, and Ward was shocked when he heard recently that Parks Canada will end the programme entirely as of this month. Prime Minister Mark Carney's government is making broad funding cuts to Canada's public service, and Parks Canada announced last week that hundreds of their employees will soon be laid off. The agency confirmed the news to the BBC, calling it a "difficult decision" to axe its sole dog handler position out of Banff National Park, one of the most rugged parts of Canada that welcomes more than four million visitors each year from around the world. It added it is part of its efforts to modernise its law enforcement branch, and that "search and rescue operations will continue to be delivered" through other means.Cutting this one role has stirred public outrage, with more than 5,000 people signing a petition since Tuesday to restore it. William Stevenson, the Conservative Member of Parliament for the Banff area who started the petition, says he welcomes tighter government spending, but that this cut could harm public safety. "How could they possibly make such a bad choice in where to cut?" he told the BBC.The BBC has asked Parks Canada about how much the canine search and rescue programme cost to administer. For 55 years, the government used rescue dogs in the Canadian Rocky Mountains who were trained to trace "everything", Ward said, from a small paper clip to shell casings to a human body. After avalanches, a common winter hazard in the area, they were called upon to search for trapped hikers or skiers underneath heavy mounds of snow."It saves probers hours and hours of standing shoulder to shoulder and poking in the snow, and also exposing themselves to secondary avalanche hazards," Ward said.In the summer, they helped find children who got lost, often after wandering away from their parents' campsites. "We lost a huge public safety and staff safety resource," he said. Other countries still rely on canines, often called "avalanche dogs", for mountain search and rescue, including Italy, external. The last dog in Parks Canada's programme, a German Shephard named Leroy, was retired in August. For the seven years that he was on the job, Leroy helped track 156 people, find 57 who were lost in the wilderness, and solve two murders in Banff.A new canine was trained and ready for duty before Parks Canada gave notice last week that the programme would be eliminated as part of recent C$145m ($104m; £78m) budget cuts to Parks Canada, local newspaper Rocky Mountain Outlook reported.Along with his petition, Stevenson also raised the issue in Canada's parliament during a late sitting on Thursday. In response, Ryan Turnball, a Liberal MP and the parliamentary secretary for finance, said the government is focused on reducing Canada's deficit and "ensuring public funds support growth, resilience and the well-being of Canadians".Stevenson said he will continue to push on the issue, and has asked for a sit-down meeting with Parks Canada's CEO. As for Ward, he hopes that the programme will soon be restored. He recalled a quote that was often uttered by an old park warden who trained him: "You can make an armpit smell like a lilac bush and you can put a man on the moon, but nothing can replace the nose of the avalanche dog."

schema.headline: Canada stops using 'avalanche dogs' for rescues in Rocky Mountains, stirring outrage

title: Russell Brand accusers 'haunted' for years by alleged crimes, court hears
description: Some of the women in Russell Brand's rape and sexual assault case have been "haunted" for years by what they allege he did to them, jurors have been t
body: Some of the women in Russell Brand's rape and sexual assault case have been "haunted" for years by what they allege he did to them, jurors have been told.In her closing speech at London's Southwark Crown Court on Friday, prosecutor Reil Karmy-Jones KC said the women had "nothing to gain" from coming forward apart from "some closure".Speaking for the defence, Polly Dyer told jurors Brand had pleaded guilty and been fined over possession of cannabis in 1995, but had no other "convictions, cautions, reprimands or warnings". Brand, 51, is on trial facing seven charges; three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one allegation of attempted indecent assault. He denies the charges.Karmy-Jones KC told the court that this case brings together six different women, none of whom knows each other.She said that while all the alleged victims have since moved on with their lives, due to this trial they have been forced to "relive what has happened to them".None of the women involved has "sought the limelight" or "any kind of publicity", she said, adding there was "no benefit to them from perhaps some closure."Referring to Brand's accusers' evidence the prosecutor said "how many said he was nice and then there was a like a personality change…"His eyes changed, he snapped, from charming to frightening to nasty," Karmy-Jones KC said.She added that the complainant's evidence had been that "he didn't listen when I said no, he didn't stop, he didn't care, pulling pushing… thrusting"."In the rape cases, he kept on going until he achieved his ultimate aim."The prosecutor also dismissed the idea that a documentary had caused the women to "re-invent" what actually happened."There is no magic force in this documentary", she added."What in fact happened was these women have realised they are not alone and have bravely come before you to tell the truth."She added: "Truth they have lived with, which in some cases has haunted them for years."She told the jury: "The experience of people raped may be something that looms a little bit larger in your mind rather than the intricacies of the outfit."The defendant couldn't really remember anything when he was interviewed, in stark contrast to now when he suddenly seems to remember all sorts of details about the week."Addressing Brand's presented change in character, Karmy-Jones KC told the court "He may now be a completely different person to the man he was between 1999 and 2009."She added: "He may well look back and not find some of his jokes funny"."He may now treat women with kindness and consent".Brand's wife Laura gave evidence yesterday, when she told the court her husband was a "kind and a wonderful father".Karmy-Jones KC called her Russell Brand's "undoubtedly lovely wife", who "bravely" gave evidence.However, she also noted that she was not with him at the time many of the alleged acts are said to have taken place."The reality is she wasn't there then, for the first five counts, she wasn't with him, nor was she with him for the final two counts.""Any contact was, I believe, sparse."In the final set of agreed facts in his trial, the court heard from Dyer about Brand's fine after he "pleaded guilty to one charge of possessing cannabis on 20 April 1995"."He received a fine. He has no other convictions, cautions, reprimands or warnings", she said.The trial continues.

schema.headline: Russell Brand accusers 'haunted' for years by alleged crimes, court hears

title: US approves sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine
description: The latest move comes after a row between Zelensky and Donald Trump earlier this month when the US eased sanctions on Russia as part of a deal to secu
body: The latest move comes after a row between Zelensky and Donald Trump earlier this month when the US eased sanctions on Russia as part of a deal to secure Russian diesel. The US president stated it was time for Ukraine to get a new leader to strike a deal to end the war with Russia. Moscow launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, having earlier seized Crimea and parts of Donbas in the east. Tensions eased after Zelensky held talks with US envoys in Oslo on 20 October.In Friday's statement, the State Department said "this proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic stability in Europe".It said "Ukraine will pay for this purchase with donations from Canada, Germany, and Norway via the JUMPSTART program and national funds, financed by the European Union's Ukraine Support Loan". The statement said the "principal contractor" would be American company Lockheed Martin, adding that "no US funds are involved in this sale".Meanwhile, at the G20 foreign ministers' meeting European diplomats protested over the presence of Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov by refusing to stand for an official photograph.The meeting is being hosted in Atlanta by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio."Let me say this directly to the Russian Foreign Minister: We all know who the aggressor in this war is," UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Lavrov at the summit, accusing his government of killing innocent civilians in Ukraine.

schema.headline: US approves sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine

title: Global nature talks reach deal but money remains an issue
description: In Armenia's capital this week a fight between politicians broke out - not the mass brawl in its parliament that was so widely documented on social me
body: In Armenia's capital this week a fight between politicians broke out - not the mass brawl in its parliament that was so widely documented on social media - but between delegates from nearly 200 countries. The world's nations have been gathered in Yerevan for nearly two weeks  negotiating, and arguing, over a new agreement on nature.Early on Saturday morning, hours after talks were due to finish, they finally agreed the key parts of a new action plan. "And that's it. Perfect," said the meeting president, Hambardzum Matevosyan. Four years earlier the same countries had signed a landmark deal committing to "halt and reverse" the decline of nature. That global deal in 2022 - the Global Biodiversity Framework - contained 24 targets including putting 30% of the world's land and seas into protection by the end of the decade.They agreed that action was urgent. The world is currently in a sixth mass extinction event with species becoming extinct at 100 times the natural rate because of human activities, scientists say.But according to the UN this week,, external the world is on track to achieve just one of those two dozen targets. As part of this week's deal, countries acknowledged they were falling behind."While not particularly exciting or detailed, it's good news that countries could reach agreement," said Catherine Weller, from environmental charity Fauna & Flora."We cannot just plod on to 2030 without a course correction; nature is critical to all life on Earth: to our economies, to our wellbeing," she added. This was echoed by Craig Bennett, CEO of The Wildlife Trusts, who told BBC News: "We are still seeing an appalling loss, threatening the collapse of ecosystems globally. We run out of words really about how serious this is."But he added "the better news is there are so many examples worldwide about how... to turn things around".Countries have put 623 million acres (252m hectares) of degraded land into protection, external - an area bigger than Greenland. Just last month the WWF praised conservation efforts which had achieved the recovery of key species including elephants, green sea turtles and tigers.Bluefin tuna comeback shows nature can recover, says WWFCountries have recognised the main barrier to accelerating those efforts is money. In 2022, they agreed they would put $30bn (£22.4bn) towards nature recovery efforts by the end of the decade, and mobilise a further $170bn from private sources.But years later many nations have been redirecting international aid to defence budgets and to deal with repeated energy shocks, such that pledges are not at the rate required to reach those targets, according to the UN. , externalAt this meeting, more than $1bn was pledged, with half of that coming from philanthropists including Leonardo DiCaprio's Re:wild organisation. Anna Ducros, a researcher at the International Institute for Environment and Development, said there had been some progress on countries committing to reducing subsidies for industries harmful to the environment."A concrete example is that governments subsidise large-scale fishing that is especially harmful for nature - for example, trawling."Ducros, who was in attendance at the talks, added: "Right now, we have the situation where governments are paying twice. "So they know that they need to increase spending on nature and climate, but at the same time, they're damaging nature."A specific funding pot, the Cali Fund, was previously set up for private companies that profit from using genetic material found in the environment to donate to. It was estimated up to $3.6bn could be raised annually -  at the start of the meeting just $10,000 had been pledged.Little progress was made on that issue - its voluntary nature makes it difficult to put pressure on companies, Bennett acknowledged."When you have countries that have rich biodiversity in them and you have companies trying to make money out of the genetic material found in those countries they should be paying those communities," he said. "That should not be controversial."One of the easier issues on the agenda was meant to be the approval of scientific reports into the state of nature. But a small group of countries, including Saudi Arabia and Russia, were reported to have frustrated that process."The attacks on science have bothered me a lot," French Ecological Transition Minister Monique Barbut was reported as saying by the AFP news agency. Next month countries will gather for the annual climate conference - COP31. Its own science body, the IPCC, has faced similar challenges in the past month with passing its own scientific reports and securing funding."This is such a blatant political move...and the IPCC is no such place for such political manoeuvring since the outputs are in humanity's interest," said Prof David Lee, from Manchester University, who has worked on previous reports.

schema.headline: Global nature talks reach deal but money remains an issue

title: South Africa vs Australia: Hosts set up epic finale - what do stats and history suggest could happen?
description: Cape Town set for classic finale – what does history suggest could happen?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Wiaan Mulder reached his century du
body: Cape Town set for classic finale – what does history suggest could happen?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Wiaan Mulder reached his century during a final-wicket partnership with Kagiso RabadaByMatthew HenryBBC Sport journalistThird Test, Cape Town (day four of five)South Africa 329 & 387: Mulder 115, Rickelton 101Australia 429: Inglis 102; Harmer 4-104Australia need 288 to winScorecardA gripping series has the finale it deserves.Having effectively began day four on 40-4, South Africa batted on and on against Australia in Cape Town to move from a position where defeat looked likely to one where a series victory is a real possibility.In being bowled out for 387 in the final over - with Ryan Rickelton making 101 and Wiaan Mulder last man out for a brilliant 115 - South Africa set the tourists a target of 288 for victory.WinViz - the tool analysts CricViz use to predict such results - gives the hosts a 54% chance of victory.If only things were that simple…History a good omen for AustraliaAustralia's target is such that should they chase it on day five, it would be the second-highest fourth-innings chase in the 62 previous Tests on this famous ground.The highest? That's a good omen for Australia.They chased 331 for a four-wicket win in an epic Test against the Proteas in 2002, when Ricky Ponting hit a brilliant 100 not out.There have been five other scores above 288 in the fourth innings at Newlands - all of which were made in defeats or when salvaging a draw.For much of the afternoon and evening sessions, as Australia's bowlers tired, this surface appeared flat enough to score.When Rickelton and Mulder applied themselves, few opportunities were created. They were able to progress to their third and fourth Test centuries respectively.It took a run out to end Rickelton's knock, after which Marco Jansen pulled to deep square leg and Gerald Coetzee was also run out - three dismissals down to batter error in a collapse of 4-61, which left South Africa nine down and 251 runs ahead.That Mulder and number 11 Kagiso Rabada flogged 36 before the close, suggested run-scoring is not impossible.Pitch turning more but batters more secureNone of those late runs were made under the pressure of a chase, however.The wicket of Simon Harmer in the final session, bowled shouldering arms by a ball from Nathan Lyon which turned back sharply showed the difficulty ahead.Harmer dismissed Travis Head, Marnus Labuschagne, Josh Inglis and Alex Carey in Australia's first innings - all recognised batters.The 37-year-old Essex legend, who once considered playing for England, will be crucial.As ever in such scenarios, the pitch will play its part.The PitchViz rating - CricViz's way of assessing the difficulty of a surface - jumped to 6.6 in the final session, comfortably the highest (thus most difficult) rating of the Test.After settling down in the morning, the ball, as would be expected as a Test progresses, was turning significantly more in the final session than at any point across the previous four days.Interestingly, however, South Africa's false shot percentage was just 11% across day four, a drop from 18% on day three.Uneven bounce has not yet been a factor but one ball to Rickelton shortly after tea also shot low.Head the key man?Intrigue is added by the fact that whoever wins this Test will end the series top of the International Cricket Council's Test rankings.One man appears to likely to play a huge part in the outcome.Faced with a target of 205 in the first Ashes Test almost a year ago, Australia opener Head thrashed a sensational 123 from 83 balls to turn a tricky chase into a riotous charge to victory over England.There was a time, between 2008 and 2019, when Australia had a poor record in situations such as these.In that period they failed in 14 of their 17 fourth-innings chases when set targets between 200 and 350.That has changed in recent years, however, with Cummins' men having pulled off pursuits of 282 and 279 since 2023, in addition to the Perth victory last year.Few sides have been better in key moments in the modern era. Saturday will provide another chance for Australia to deliver under pressure.

schema.headline: South Africa vs Australia: Hosts set up epic finale - what do stats and history suggest could happen?

title: Crypto giant Binance attempting to recover $6.3bn stolen in hack linked to North Korea
description: Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has frozen around half of the funds stolen in a "complex" hack, after $6.3bn (£4.7bn) wa
body: Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has frozen around half of the funds stolen in a "complex" hack, after $6.3bn (£4.7bn) was accessed in what is believed to be a record heist.The firm said $3bn of its stolen digital assets had been secured - but many were still in the hands of unidentified hackers. It initially thought an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing unauthorised withdrawals, but later said the attack was wider.Several analytics firms have linked the hack, which eclipses a $1.5bn (£1.12bn) heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025, to a North Korean hacking unit.The US Secret Service said it was "working around the clock" "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover" stolen funds.America's lead federal agency for investigating financial crimes added that it would "identify the cyber criminals responsible and bring them to justice", while Binance also said it was working with the FBI.While Binance said its US-facing exchange was unaffected, the US would still have jurisdiction to investigate the hack and help track down stolen funds - an effort which generally involves a global law enforcement effort.The hack also involved some US-linked assets, such as stablecoins Tether and Circle – cryptocurrencies pegged to the dollar.Binance told its users "your money is safe, and we're covering every loss".It had initially suspended all deposits and withdrawals - but then said in an update that "deposits remain unaffected".Binance's co-CEO Richard Teng said: "This was not carried out by one person. Our initial investigation suggested that the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop, however our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach."Teng also describes how the hackers used "a self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and traces as they went, making it more difficult for us to trace and investigate".Initially, the company had indicated the breach "may have started with a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop" but later statements have pointed to a broader breach.In a later update, the firm said it had "set aside" more than $6.34B in company funds to cover the stolen assets and was "actively buying" a range of crypto tokens.The Binance hack spooked cryptocurrency markets on Friday. The price of Bitcoin was down 5% to $76,800 in Friday afternoon trading in New York.Cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase was down 12% as investors also reacted to earnings results in which the firm reported revenue slightly below expectations. Robinhood, a financial services company that trades in cryptocurrency, was down 7.8%.Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide.The company said in 2024 that it had more than $160bn in assets under its custody.A lot of the fear right now from Binance users - and the crypto industry at large - is whether or not Binance will actually be capable of covering this enormous financial loss.The company has said repeatedly that customer funds will be covered and that the firm is strong enough to weather the storm.But crypto history watchers have been pointing out online that this is exactly the kind of message that FTX CEO Sam Bankman-Fried gave before his crypto exchange collapsed in 2022, leading to huge losses for customers and the industry.Several experts have warned customers not to regard Binance's promise to cover losses as legally binding and said they may need to pursue litigation to recover them.Daniel Tunkel, of the London-based Edwin Coe law firm, said that would "come down to what [customers] have been promised in their contracts", and "where Binance can be sued for non-performance, if it comes to it".Binance has been subject of regulatory scrutiny around the world.Meanwhile, AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said that several elements of the attack resembled earlier North Korean-linked incidents, including the Bybit hack.In the last five years the crypto industry has been beset by enormous losses from hackers.In nearly all cases investigators have blamed hackers from North Korea, pointing to the infamous Lazarus Group - also know as TraderTraitor. The names refer to clusters of cyber criminals accused of working directly for the regime.Chainalysis, a crypto analytics firm, said it had "high confidence" that a North Korean is linked to the hack.North Korea is an impoverished country with very little industry and heavy international sanctions and experts say the regime uses cyber crime as a way to bring money in.North Korea has always denied this, but the wealth of evidence from cryptocurrency flow analysis and insider interviews from defectors is compelling. It makes North Korea likely to be the only nation that uses hacking as a way to raise public funds.

schema.headline: Crypto giant Binance attempting to recover $6.3bn stolen in hack linked to North Korea

title: Beat Luke Littler: Farron Sherrock upsets world champion to claim £501,000 prize
description: Fallon Sherrock defeated reigning world champion Luke Littler in one leg of darts on Friday to win £501,000.Broadcast live globally on Netflix, Beat L
body: Fallon Sherrock defeated reigning world champion Luke Littler in one leg of darts on Friday to win £501,000.Broadcast live globally on Netflix, Beat Luke Littler featured a host of amateur players taking on world number one Littler in a one-leg face-off at Manchester Central.Players could not be members of the PDC Tour, meaning Sherrock, who became the first female player to beat a male opponent at the PDC World Championship on her way to the last 32 in December 2019, was allowed to compete.After Littler had defeated 14 amateurs, some as young as 14, he was always going to have a tough task against 32-year-old Sherrock, a player who has won 21 times on the PDC Women's Series.She had been closest to the bull to start first and hit a 180, only the third maximum of the night, before taking out double 20 to clinch the prize.Sherrock, whose son Rory was among the crowd, said: "It's insane, I can't put it into words of what it means, especially having Rory here - it's his first time at anything and he has seen me win."It's a great moment and I will memorise this forever. Give me an opportunity and I will take it every time. I'm really proud of myself, I rise to the occasion."Nineteen-year-old Littler, who has won the PDC World Championship in both the past two events, said: "Brilliant, that's what one person had to do - win the bull and go out in 15 [darts] and that's what she did, world class."The packed crowd in Manchester was in boisterous mood with many fans in fancy dress, but this was darts with a difference.There had been 25,000 applicants who had entered the competition.The first stage saw players have to get down from 501 in 24 darts or less, with those successful then facing a three-person interview panel, including 16-time world champion Phil Taylor, PDC president Barry Hearn and darts television pundit Laura Turner.Twenty players were due to play at the event. Sixteen were selected outright, while the eight most experienced players were paired off, with Netflix viewers voting on which one should be able to compete.Sherrock was in the vote against Germany's Jarod Becker, but collected 75% of the votes to get the chance to face Littler.She had picked up £25,000 for reaching round three of the PDC World Championship at Alexandra Palace seven years ago after beating Ted Evetts and Mensur Suljovic before losing to Chris Dobey.Her achievement saw her nicknamed 'The Queen of the Palace' and she was also awarded an MBE for her services to darts in 2023.Sherrock's victory over Littler meant the event immediately ended, meaning the five remaining amateurs were unable to get their shot at the £501,000 prize.While Sherrock was celebrating, Ireland's 'Fierce' Pearse Mackle, a 21-year-old university student from County Cavan, was left wondering what could have been.Mackle, who competes on PDC's Development Tour, was the eighth competitor and failed to hit a match-winning bullseye, instead finding the nine, and his life-changing moment came and went.He was the only other player, apart from Sherrock, to cause Littler a fright.For most of the night, Littler cruised through the competition as he went in search of the £501,000, which he had said he would donate to charity.With former England footballer Gary Lineker hosting and with comedian Lee Mack and television presenter Richard Osman joining Turner as part of the punditry team, this was a night to bring darts to a new audience.The first challenger was 16-year-old Kasey Smith from Manchester, but Littler showed he was in no mood to mess about, hitting treble 20s against her with his first two darts on his way to an easy win.Some of Littler's opponents had never played a competitive game of darts, although everyone was keen to make the most of the experience.With John McDonald, who retired as the main PDC master of ceremonies after the 2026 World Championship final, announcing the players before their elaborate walk-ons, this was a fun event, although most players came nowhere near beating Littler.But there were still entertaining moments. Fourteen-year-old Jayden Walker, a year 10 pupil from Dorset, threw off a school blazer and tie to reveal his darts outfit and, as the third-highest ranked player, threatened to cause a huge shock.But Littler raised his game when he needed to, hitting a maximum 180 followed by a 158 checkout, the highest of the night, to defeat his fellow teenager in only 12 darts.Taylon Forrester, 18, described himself as a "binman who works with his dad" and he jumped out of a dumpster on his way to the oche. Other entrants included Zac Spain, a jockey from Melbourne, Australia, Frenchman Theodore Wallich, who dubbed himself the 'Moustache Kid', 57-year-old Mark Pooke, another 14-year-old in Makinley Cooper-Johnson and Will Kemp, back playing after a heart attack earlier this year.But Sherrock, whose participation in the competition had been questioned because of her past achievements in the sport, was the real winner, even if she had been described by Lineker as a "hairdresser from Milton Keynes".With Littler on stage for more than two hours, he inevitably tired with his standard dropping and Sherrock was the one to take advantage, winning in a 15-dart leg in match number 15.Hearn reappeared to present Sherrock with a huge cheque for her life-changing victory to end a surreal night of action.

schema.headline: Beat Luke Littler: Farron Sherrock upsets world champion to claim £501,000 prize

title: Binance hack - who is behind it, is my money safe and what we know so far
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByLaura CressTechnology reporterBinance, the world's largest crypto exchange, has been hit by what is believed to be the lar
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByLaura CressTechnology reporterBinance, the world's largest crypto exchange, has been hit by what is believed to be the largest crypto hack ever at $6.3bn (£4.7bn).Crypto is a type of digital asset which does not exist physically like cash or coins. Instead, people use digital wallets on their smartphones or computers to access and manage it.Richard Teng, Binance's co-chief executive officer, said it is working with the authorities to work out what has happened and it will cover all losses.Here's what we know so far.What is Binance?Binance is the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange by trading volume, where people can buy, sell and trade digital currencies, like Bitcoin, as well as deposit and withdraw them.It was founded in China in 2017 and has hundreds of millions of registered users worldwide.The exchange has come under scrutiny over the past few years - notably in 2023, when its then-chief executive, Changpeng Zhao, resigned after pleading guilty to money laundering violations.Last year, a lawsuit in the US accused the company of helping send millions of dollars to US-designated terrorist organisations.In 2024, the company said it has more than $160bn in assets.How did the hack happen?The hack happened to Binance's global centralised exchange, Binance.com. Binance.us, which provides trading services specifically for US residents, said it has not been affected by the issue.In an initial announcement, Teng said: "Our initial investigation suggests this security incident may have started with a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop. "That gave an attacker access to a service container, where they submitted unauthorised withdrawal transactions."He said the hack "was not a simple 'one-click' action" but a "more complex attack process".Raghu Nandakumara, vice president of industry strategy at cybersecurity platform Illumio, said this could mean an engineer was "talked into taking a test" and malware - malicious software – "landed on their laptop while they did it".Because the laptop already had sufficient security privileges, Nandakumara said early reports suggest it became "the attacker's route straight into production, and from there to the wallets".Teng has since said the hack was "not carried out by one person" and the hackers used sophisticated methods to hide their tracks, such as a "self-destruct mechanism". "You can build a vault with mathematical firewalls, but if the individual holding the keys can be duped, the vault is opened," said Dr Clive Summerfield, head of FARx, a biometrics in AI security company.Image source, Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, Binance co-chief executive officer Richard Teng speaks at a conferenceWho is behind the hack?It is not yet known who is behind the attack, but some analytics firms have pointed to North Korea - though this has not been confirmed.AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said in a report several elements of the Binance attack resembled earlier incidents linked to the territory, including a $1.5bn (£1.1bn) hack on the ByBit exchange in 2025.These previous attacks have been linked to a cluster of cyber-criminals accused of working directly for the regime called the Lazarus Group - also known as TraderTraitor. North Korean foreign policy expert Dr Edward Howell, from the University of Oxford, has told the BBC that Pyongyang "has a long history of using cyber warfare to extract cash".Howell said North Korea "basically has a state-run cyber warfare agency", which it uses "to fund its weapons of mass destruction programmes" and as a "slush fund" for its leader Kim Jong Un's regime.Howell added that as of the current day "about 40 – 50% of North Korea's weapons of mass destruction programmes are funded by cyber and crypto-currency warfare".North Korea has always denied any involvement in these attacks; Binance has not directly responded to BBC queries about the incident's potential links to the area.What does it mean for Binance users?In his earlier statement, Teng said Binance users' funds are safe and, as a precaution, all deposits and withdrawals had been temporarily suspended.He said the firm would cover all losses from its emergency reserve set up for such situations, and make up the rest with company funds.Binance said it had been working with partners to freeze the affected assets, with around $3bn reportedly located so far. Teng said concerned users can check funds on their Binance accounts. Experts suggest doing so through the official app and website, and to reach out to the company's customer service with any questions. Users from other crypto platforms have also been warned to be wary of hackers seeking to exploit the situation.Marijus Briedis, NordVPN's chief technology officer, said people should be on the lookout for things such as "an email claiming your funds are at risk", "a fake support account offering help" or "a message urging you to move your cryptocurrency to a 'safe' wallet"."Check updates through the Binance app or a website address you already trust," he said. "Avoid links in unsolicited messages, and never give anyone your password, verification codes or wallet recovery phrase."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Binance.us said it had not been affected by the issueWhat does this mean for cryptocurrency and the wider financial system?Jennifer Craven, an international commercial fraud expert at the law firm Pinsent Masons, said the repercussions of the hack could "extend well beyond Binance"."More broadly, the incident exposes the fragility of parts of the crypto ecosystem," she said. "If a platform as sophisticated as Binance can suffer a serious attack, regulators will inevitably ask what that means for smaller, less mature platforms and currencies."She said the attack would likely accelerate scrutiny of how the sector protects both its infrastructure and its customers. Although there is no evidence yet that AI was used in this attack, it fits into a much wider concern in the financial industry of whether AI agents could potentially identify weaknesses in software and work out how to exploit them much faster than human hackers.The Bank of England has warned, external this could leave institutions struggling to fix vulnerabilities before attackers take advantage of them.How many people use cryptocurrency?Crypto has become an increasingly popular way of investing and transferring money online, partly because, unlike traditional currencies, it is not controlled by central banks or governments.This makes it popular for people who think decentralisation can bring financial freedom.But it also makes it extremely volatile, with it rising and falling in value at the whim of buyers and sellers.According to Solcard, a crypto-funded prepaid payment and virtual card platform, somewhere between 560 million and 741 million people own crypto worldwide in 2026.

schema.headline: Binance hack - who is behind it, is my money safe and what we know so far

title: 'Respected and beloved': Tributes pour in for Sir Patrick Stewart
description: Dame Judi Dench said she was "shocked" and "very sad" to hear of Sir Patrick's death, adding: "He's never been one of those actors who never felt like
body: Dame Judi Dench said she was "shocked" and "very sad" to hear of Sir Patrick's death, adding: "He's never been one of those actors who never felt like it that night, he was always very, very committed... He'll be much missed and he was much admired."George Takei, who played Hikaru Sulu in Star Trek, said the actor "inspired a whole next generation of star-gazers who looked longingly ahead to a brighter future for all humanity".Sir Patrick would later be celebrated for his portrayal of Professor Charles Xavier - most commonly known as Professor X - in the X-Men film franchise.Hugh Jackman, who starred alongside him in the franchise, called him a "tremendous friend and man", saying: "We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today."Sir Ian, a longtime friend of his X-Men co-star, who officiated his wedding in 2013, said Sir Patrick was "defined by being born and bred in Yorkshire"."You could hear it in his accented voice and in the stern honesty with which he told you what he thought and felt. Yorkshiremen have no truck with half-truths or avoidance of big issues."Sir Ian recalled first meeting Sir Patrick as young actors in the Royal Shakespeare Company (RSC) and how he had expressed caution over him taking on the Star Trek role."He took the risk and thank goodness for us all that he did," said Sir Ian, who appeared with Sir Patrick in a 2009 theatre production of Waiting for Godot.He added that while the US had become Sir Patrick's "adopted home", he "never forsook his origins" growing up in Yorkshire, and said "the proudest achievement of the most respected and beloved actor of his generation on either side of the Atlantic, was his appointment as chancellor of Huddersfield University".Sir Ian noted that Sir Patrick's final film appearance will be as Professor X in the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday film. Marvel Studios described him as "a singular talent, a generous collaborator and a true gentleman".The Academy dubbed his voice "unmistakable", adding: "Whether commanding the bridge of the Enterprise or guiding a generation of young mutants, Sir Patrick Stewart brought a tenderness to his characters that made us feel we knew them."Sir Patrick died on Wednesday "in the loving care of his wife", a statement from his family said. "We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace," it added.The veteran actor is survived by his wife, Sunny Ozell, as well as by his two adult children from his first marriage, Daniel and Sophie Stewart.Dame Harriet Walter, who first met Sir Patrick in his theatre days more than 40 years ago, said his passing was like a "huge giant tree has fallen in the forest"."He had fire in his eyes and you were absolutely in the room with him," the Succession actress told BBC Newsnight. "I've never heard a bad word against him. And I think the world's going to be very poor without him."Theatres in London's West End will dim their lights for two minutes on 3 November in his honour.  Hannah Essex, co-chief of the Society of London Theatre and UK Theatre, called him "one of the greatest stage actors this country has ever seen".As well as having roles in films such as Safe House, Robin Hood: Men in Tights and the original Dune, Sir Patrick continued to appear on TV throughout his career, making guest appearances on Frasier, Futurama and the Simpsons.US actor and animator Seth MacFarlane, who grew up as a fan of Sir Patrick, said he was "gifted the privilege of becoming a colleague and friend" as they worked together on Family Guy, American Dad! and Ted. MacFarlane described him as a "rare actor who could take any bit of dialogue and elevate it, making a good writer sound great and a great writer sound masterful".Comedian Ricky Gervais, whose BBC programme Extras Sir Patrick guest starred in, described him as a "legend".Sharing a video of the pair giggling in a set of bloopers for the series, Gervais said: "I still can't believe he agreed to do this scene. And he didn't even mind when I ruined every take."Sir Patrick was a lifelong supporter of English Football League club Huddersfield Town, which called him a "titan of his craft"."Fiercely proud of his Yorkshire roots, Sir Patrick was a Terrier in every sense, and we're proud to have counted him as one of our own," the club added.Alzheimer's is the most common type of dementia, while Lewy Body Dementia is another common form caused by abnormal protein deposits, which cause a loss of cognitive function.The Alzheimer's Society CEO Michelle Dyson said Sir Patrick was an "extraordinarily talented and much-loved actor, admired by millions around the world", adding: "His death is a heartbreaking reminder of the devastating impact dementia has on people and families across the globe."The actor became a campaigner on domestic violence in later life, including becoming an ambassador for domestic abuse charity Refuge in 2007, after witnessing his mother suffer violence at the hands of his father.Hetti Barkworth-Nanton, Refuge's board chair, said it had been a privilege to "watch his endless devotion" to the cause, adding that he "broke down barriers and taboos on the subject".Andy Burnham considered Sir Patrick to be "one of the very best" who "never forgot his working-class Yorkshire roots"."He brought joy to millions," the prime minister's spokesman said on his behalf. "He always stood up for what he believed in, including through his campaigning to help those affected by domestic violence.

schema.headline: 'Respected and beloved': Tributes pour in for Sir Patrick Stewart

title: Lèse majesté: Arnon Nampa questioned Thailand's monarchy dressed as Harry Potter. Now he's in jail for 34 years
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Arnon Nampa dressed as Harry Potter at the protest in August 2020 ByJonathan HeadSouth East Asia correspondentRepo
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Arnon Nampa dressed as Harry Potter at the protest in August 2020 ByJonathan HeadSouth East Asia correspondentReporting fromBangkokEven before they come through the door, you can hear the prisoners walking towards the courtroom, the shackles round their ankles clinking with each step.The five who walk into the courtroom are familiar with the routine; they are facing multiple criminal prosecutions and have spent much of the past five years going back and forth to court.One of them, a small, bespectacled man with greying hair, opens his arms to hold his three-year-old son, who has been brought to court by his partner to see him.This is Arnon Nampa, a 42-year-old human rights lawyer. His offence was to call for Thailand's powerful monarchy to be scrutinised and held accountable. He did this dressed as the eponymous young wizard at a Harry Potter-themed demonstration in central Bangkok in 2020.On Friday a court in Bangkok sentenced him to two years and eight months for violating Thailand's lèse majesté law, or article 112, under which more people have been jailed for perceived insults against the royal family than in all the other countries that have such laws combined.This is just one out of 14 cases brought against Arnon under the same charge, bringing the cumulative sentence he has received so far to more than 34 years. The verdict in two cases is still pending."To me, this isn't a surprise," he later told reporters. "If the country was more open, we would be able to talk about these issues freely."Image source, Arnon Nampa's familyImage caption, A drawing by Arnon Nampa's 10-year-old daughter showing her father in prisonThe past six years have seen the most extensive use of lèse majesté in Thai history, in response to unprecedented student protests in 2020 which for the first time called for a public discussion of the role of the monarchy. Two hundred and ninety-four people, including 20 under the age of 18, have been prosecuted, receiving prison sentences of up to 50 years. Dozens of them are still on trial.Most of those charged under this law are denied bail and kept in jail, even though their court cases can last several years. The standard defence of the law given by Thai officials is that it "reflects the culture and history of Thailand, where the monarchy is one of the main pillars of the nation, highly revered by the majority of Thai people".Article 112 of the Thai criminal code simply reads, "Whoever defames, insults or threatens the King, the Queen, the Heir-apparent or the Regent, shall be punished with imprisonment of three to 15 years."In practice, though, the law has been interpreted to cover a much wider range of comment about the monarchy, and a much wider range of figures. Saying anything negative about any member of the royal family, about the institution of the monarchy, even about long deceased kings, or in one case, the king's dog, has resulted in prosecutions."If you ask me what the text of the law says, I can tell you," says Akarachai Chaimaneekarakate, assistant director of Thai Lawyers for Human Rights, which helps defend those accused of breaking it. "If you ask me how the courts interpret the words "defame" or "insult", I don't think I can give you a definition, because it's so ambiguous, it's so vague. Even questioning the law itself, for example, can constitute lèse majesté under Section 112."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Arnon at a protest in 2023From his cell in the Bangkok Remand Prison, where he has been for the last three years, Arnon has been writing to his young daughter and son."Dear Pran and Karl, my beloved children,The winter wind has not only brought us cool weather, but also brings back stories from the past. I miss the time we travelled outside Bangkok that first winter after Karl came into this world. It was such a magical time for me. I shall miss it every winter I spend here until I regain my freedom." Hearings like the one Arnon attended weeks before Friday's verdict are the only times he has seen Karl since he was a baby.Karl is shy at first, but soon he's happy to be picked up and shown off to the other prisoners. His 10-year-old sister Pran sometimes visits their father in prison, and often draws and paints him.But Arnon and Lookwa, his partner, think Karl is too young to visit. For now, Karl thinks the court is just where his dad works. A group of supporters has come too, filling the little courtroom. They mingle cheerfully with the prisoners, laughing and exchanging gossip before the judges walk in to start the hearing. It is an improbably informal setting for men facing one of the most feared charges in Thailand.Image source, Arnon Nampa's familyImage caption, Arnon's family, drawn by his daughter, titled "heading to court". Her mum is carrying a poster that says, "Free my dad"The effect of the law has been to smother any public discussion about the monarchy. Until six years ago, opinions on it were only ever whispered in private. In one notorious case a taxi driver was jailed because a passenger reported what he had said while riding in his cab.That changed on 3 August 2020.That year younger Thais had become increasingly frustrated with the conservative government led by coup-leader Gen Prayuth Chan-ocha. The year before millions had given their votes to a new party, Future Forward, which promised sweeping reforms, but in February 2020, the Constitutional Court dissolved the party on a technicality. The arrival of the Covid pandemic prevented any protests for three months, but as infections in Thailand started to fall, students began holding rallies calling for an end to the military's role in politics. Arnon Nampa argued this did not go far enough.In the garb of Harry Potter, he gave a speech saying it was time to talk about the opaque power and wealth of the monarchy. He criticised King Vajiralongkorn's decision to take personal control of the vast assets held by the Crown Property Bureau, and over important units of the army.In a single speech Arnon shattered a taboo which had hung over Thai society for the whole of its modern history. For the rest of that year the student-led protests continued, with increasingly bold demands for changes to the monarchy.At the time, the use of the lèse majesté law had been suspended for three years. Sources close to the palace have in the past acknowledged that the negative publicity generated by lèse majesté convictions might do more harm than good.But the protests forced a hasty reassessment. From the end of 2020 prosecutions under the law restarted and accelerated. Dozens of young activists have fled into exile to avoid being jailed.Image source, Arnon Nampa's familyImage caption, Arnon's reunion with his family, as drawn by his daughterOne of them is Supitcha "Melinn" Chailom. The 24-year-old from Chiang Mai in northern Thailand lives in Montreal, a fugitive from four 112 charges which have been filed against her.She was an 18-year-old school girl when she stood up and made a speech at a protest in Chiang Mai University, just three weeks after Arnon Nampa's call for reform of the monarchy.A local photographer captured the moment she raised her hand in the three-finger Hunger Games salute, eliciting loud cheers from the crowd. It became one of the defining images of the protests, and propelled Melinn to nationwide fame. She travelled up and down the country as one of the leading voices in the movement, demanding changes to Thailand's old-fashioned education system, conducting polls on what people thought of the monarchy."I love playing games, and I dreamed of being a game designer," she told me from Canada. But her parents did not approve."I felt that, as a young person, I could not question, or have a discussion with people older than me. The monarchy gave me the same vibe."In November 2020 Melinn joined a protest in the southern city of Hat Yai, where she gave a speech comparing the royal treatment given to the king's dog with that of ordinary people. Nine months later the police delivered a summons to her home charging her with lèse majesté."It was a shock. I wasn't expecting it because I only talked about the dog. It was during Covid when the police came to my home with the summons, so they knew my parents would be there with me. They tried to stay calm, but I nearly lost my mind."Image source, GoodmondayshootImage caption, Melinn doing the three-finger salute in August 2020Her family tried to persuade her to co-operate with the authorities, to admit her wrongdoing. But Melinn refused.She joined a movement calling itself Thalu Wang, which translates as "breaking through the palace". Instead of giving speeches, they came up with stunts like holding polls on the street, asking people what they thought of royal motorcades holding up the traffic, or whether they believed the monarchy had too much power."We knew the risks, but we thought it would be safer just conducting a poll. It turns out it was not."She was given two more lèse majesté charges in 2022, and detained before being released on bail. She had to wear an electronic monitor on her ankle and was barred from leaving her home between 4pm and 6am. Her parents were forced to sign a document promising to inform on her. She was facing decades in jail. Melinn decided she had no choice. With a friend she fled Thailand and eventually got asylum in Canada.Image source, Arnon Nampa's familyImage caption, A painting by Arnon's daughter titled "my dad's feelings"Article 112 is on paper just a law, like any other, passed by Thai parliament, which can, theoretically, be amended by elected MPs. In fact it has been amended in the past, notably in 1976 when the punishment for breaking it was increased to between three and 15 years in prison.But today the Constitutional Court has decreed that the law itself, like the institution it protects, is untouchable. The reformist Move Forward party - the successor of Future Forward - was dissolved in 2024, and its leader banned from politics, merely for proposing that the punishments be less harsh. And the courts make it very difficult for those charged under it to defend themselves."In many cases, like the one against Arnon Nampa, prosecutors accuse the defendant of lying about the monarchy," says Chaimaneekarakate, the lawyer. "But when we ask the judge to subpoena documents or witnesses who could show the truth of what the defendant says, the judge refuses to do it. When one lawyer protested against the court deciding that the trial would be held in secret, she was warned by the judge to be quiet or face a contempt of court charge."He says judges sometimes criticise the young activists over their alleged actions even before the trial has started.Image source, Arnon NampaImage caption, Arnon has been writing letters to his children since he was jailed three years agoAs the one who ignited the debate about the monarchy Arnon appears to be getting the harshest punishment. Despite the formidable odds stacked against him he still prepares carefully for every court appearance, taking part in his own defence and helping other inmates with theirs. This isn't easy; he is not allowed to bring any of his written notes, and must memorise all his arguments.The judges object to him playing the part of a lawyer in his regulation-brown prison shorts, his feet bare and shackled. But it does give him an opportunity to see his family.The letters he writes are the only other way he stays in touch with them. He may spend his entire life in prison. He wants his children to know him, and to understand, when they are older, why he chose to challenge the system and lose his freedom."Since the first day that we made up our mind to take up this mission, we knew of the dangers. Speaking the truth is not difficult. What is difficult is speaking a forbidden truth. I remember well that on the evening of 3 August 2020, after speaking at the Harry Potter event, I felt very good, content, and relieved to have finally begun speaking about the truth, in public," he wrote to his family last year.Earlier this year, he wrote: "Living here is a struggle. But it is just a dot in the bigger picture of our movement's struggle. We must play a part in writing our own history. Become a drop of water that will one day become an ocean."

schema.headline: Lèse majesté: Arnon Nampa questioned Thailand's monarchy dressed as Harry Potter. Now he's in jail for 34 years

title: Eddie Howe to Man Utd? The fans, the finances, the football structure
description: What Howe could bring to Man Utd - and what are the challenges?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Eddie Howe has been out of work since leaving
body: What Howe could bring to Man Utd - and what are the challenges?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Eddie Howe has been out of work since leaving Newcastle United in the summerBySenior football correspondentWhen Sir Jim Ratcliffe became a co-owner of Manchester United in 2024, much of the narrative centred on his desire to rebuild the club around a British core.Given the expense of buying homegrown players, and the difficulties Michael Carrick -  the first permanent British managerial appointment of the Ineos era - has faced this season, perhaps Ratcliffe is rethinking.But if Carrick fails to stop the rot and loses his job, United are already considering the merits of appointing another British coach - albeit one who is more experienced.That Eddie Howe is a contender for a job that remains one of the most high-profile in world football isn't hard to fathom.Speak to those who have worked alongside Howe and they describe a man whose track record of improving players is a direct result of his relentless approach on the training field.They will also tell you Howe is someone who places an unwavering importance on the methodology of setting a winning culture.Howe may lack experience at one of the traditional top-six clubs, but his body of work at Bournemouth and Newcastle is impressive.Having been appointed Bournemouth boss with the club facing relegation from League Two in January 2009, Howe led them to the Premier League in 2015. He went on to establish the Cherries as a top-flight club before leaving - for a second time - in 2020.In 2021, Howe was appointed Newcastle manager. He led them from relegation trouble to qualification for the Champions League on two occasions and won the EFL Cup - the club's first trophy in 56 years - in 2025.Mixed reception to Howe linksOf course, managing Manchester United is an altogether different proposition.Indeed, Howe's emergence as a potential successor to Carrick has been greeted with negativity in some circles.Sections of the fanbase have been vocal on social media with their opinion that Howe isn't a big enough name to replace Carrick.Former United players Paul Scholes and Nicky Butt also fell short of providing their backing to Howe on their podcast, though it is worth pointing out they spoke in favour of the 48-year-old's potential appointment when Ruben Amorim was sacked in January.Ex-captain Roy Keane is among those to have backed Howe as a possible successor to Carrick, and other former top-flight players - including Darren Bent, Gareth Barry and Jack Wilshere - have also touted him as the man for the job.Of course, if you look hard enough you'll find voices for and against every potential manager, and it will be up to United chief executive Omar Berrada, sporting director Jason Wilcox and director of recruitment Christopher Vivell to weigh up how they proceed.Their first decision will be what happens with Carrick, and Saturday's match against Chelsea is likely to have a bearing on how United move forward.Figure caption, 'I don't need any assurances'Finances a factor in Carrick's futureIf Carrick does depart, finances will inevitably be a factor.The former Middlesbrough boss and his staff will need to be paid up before United even get to factoring in the monetary commitment towards their next head coach.While the details of Howe's agreement with Newcastle when he left in the summer remain confidential, it is understood that as things stand any club or national team would be required to pay a seven-figure compensation fee to the Magpies. Multiple sources have told BBC Sport that Newcastle - with a view to protecting themselves against Howe walking straight into another club - reached an agreement over a compensation structure that decreases over time.It is understood that figure started at £6m but has already reduced by half.The compensation payments have an expiry date - understood to be before the end of the season - at which point he can be appointed for nothing.Of course, in an industry in which astronomical figures are the norm, the prospect of paying a maximum of £3m for Howe may not be too problematic.That said, given the amount Manchester United have spent on hiring and firing managers in recent years, it is understandable if Berrada and Wilcox want to keep costs down.Would Howe fit Man Utd's footballing structure? As well as the doubts from some supporters about Howe's potential appointment, there has also been conjecture over how he would fit in United's footballing structure.At both Bournemouth and Newcastle, Howe developed a strong powerbase in all aspects of the footballing department - including recruitment.That dynamic wasn't without financial benefit to Howe's employers.The likes of Nathan Ake, Callum Wilson and Tyrone Mings were all signed by Howe at Bournemouth - and sold for a big profit by the Cherries.At Newcastle, meanwhile, Howe was instrumental in the signings of Bruno Guimarares, Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and Alexander Isak - all of whom were sold for more than they joined for. Dan Burn, Lewis Hall and Tino Livramento are among those to have developed into full England internationals under his coaching.But with a football management structure at Old Trafford that includes Berrada, Wilcox and Vivell, it is likely that Howe - at least not immediately - would not be afforded the same level of autonomy.Howe, though, is on record saying he is happy to work alongside sporting directors, and has a track record of doing so - firstly at Bournemouth under Richard Hughes, then chief executive Neill Blake.At Newcastle, he worked closely with senior management figures Dan Ashworth, Amanda Staveley and Mehrdad Ghodoussi - so fitting into Manchester United's structure wouldn't be drastically different.Whether he would want the job given the challenges, we may never know. And ultimately it is the opinion of Manchester United's decision-makers that will truly matter.'An obvious contender to replace Carrick' - analysisByChief football news reporterHowe is an obvious contender for the Manchester United job, just as he would be if the England head coach's position became available.Whether he is offered it or not will give a clear indication about the path United are going down.Director of football Jason Wilcox is thought to favour the 48-year-old, with director of recruitment Christopher Vivell preferring former Bayern Munich and Germany coach Julian Nagelsmann.Ultimately, their recommendations will be assessed by chief executive Omar Berrada, with minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe and co-chairs Joel and Avram Glazer having the final say.It is not completely clear where the negativity about Howe moving to Old Trafford comes from, other than Wilcox being targeted by Manchester United fans during the 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth. In the current managerial climate, few managers get the chance to build a body of work at one club over a number of years as, for instance, Sir Alex Ferguson did at Aberdeen before he moved south in November 1986.There is clearly a general disillusionment among the club's matchgoing fans around the football decisions taken since Ratcliffe bought his minority stake in early 2024, but Erik ten Hag, Ruben Amorim and Michael Carrick have all been backed.Some say no manager can succeed at United with the structure as it is, and it is clear whoever is in charge needs to mould together a squad bought by six permanent managers, most of whom have differing playing styles.

schema.headline: Eddie Howe to Man Utd? The fans, the finances, the football structure

title: 'The necktie is dead': How US midterm candidates are dressing for votes
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByNardine SaadUS reporterAs Americans prepare to vote in the US midterm elections, candidates with their eye on Congress are
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByNardine SaadUS reporterAs Americans prepare to vote in the US midterm elections, candidates with their eye on Congress are not just competing on policy.In our social media age, they're using their personal style to attract attention and project their message. Their clothing has become a measure of their authenticity and appeal."Politicians are dressing for two jobs at once: to look capable of holding office but to also look connected to the people they want to represent," said Joe Zee, a celebrity fashion stylist.From Alaska to Texas, here is a look at how some candidates have been standing out on the campaign trail.Dressing like their stateSome candidates, like Democrat Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, who represents Washington's 3rd Congressional District, are embracing a relaxed, outdoorsy image.The former car repair shop owner is up for re-election on a platform focused on support for small businesses and working families, after capturing a Republican-held seat in her state in 2022. She favours low fuss, low-key work jackets, flannel shirts, jeans and practical footwear.Robert Ordway, conservative public policy adviser and former owner of Capitol Hill Clothiers, says Gluesenkamp Perez is probably the most "spot-on" when it comes to "authenticity and where you come from"."Also it really vibes with the Pacific Northwest, which has trees and forests and a little bit more of an outdoor vibe," he says.Her style also "shepherds a message championing the working class", says Tashira Halyard, an attorney, content creator, and public policy expert based in Washington DC.Image source, BBC NewsImage caption, Gluesenkamp Perez chooses a workwear-inspired wardrobeDemocratic lawmaker Mary Peltola, running for a Senate seat in the battleground state of Alaska, takes a similar approach.She made headlines for wearing traditional boots of the Yup'ik people while being sworn in as a congresswoman in 2022.During this election cycle, her rugged outdoor gear nods to her days working on a fishing boat on Alaska's Kuskokwim River and her "fish, family and freedom" campaign slogan.The flannels, puffer jackets and indigenous-inspired details seem designed to remind voters that Peltola is a native (and Native) Alaskan, says conservative author and journalist Bonnie Kristian.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Mary Peltola wore the traditional footwear of the Yup'ik people when she was sworn inPatriotism on their sleevesOther candidates, such as Republican Senate candidate Ashley Hinson of Iowa, have been opting for a bolder, patriotic image.While polished and conservative, her style of dress has included classic, arguably nostalgic touches, including denim and bandanas for more casual appearances.In a tight race against her Democratic opponent, Hinson has tried to separate herself from specific policy decisions made by the Trump administration but has still expressed loyalty to the president.She slipped into pumps with the American flag bedazzled across them at a primary election party in Iowa in June. The look, reminiscent of the style worn by Trump supporters at rallies, is quintessential American patriotism, according to Halyard."Ashley's American flag high heels, denim dress and bright red blouse worn with a bandana around her neck are classic Americana," she says."It's this idea that… I'm literally going to wear my patriotism on my sleeve."Image source, BBC NewsImage caption, Ashley Hinson's campaign style is inspired by the American flag Journalist Bonnie Kristian says there is "a strategic advantage" to Hinson's look, one in which she is "cultivating a visual identity that cannot possibly be misinterpreted" in an era where social media presence, if only for a split second, is crucial."Her denim dress, red bandana and sparkly American flag shoes all signal that she's a Republican wooing rural voters - and indeed she is."Tie off, cowboy boots onOnce a reliable Republican stronghold, Texas has become a battleground between top prosecutor Ken Paxton, 63, who was controversially endorsed by Trump over a longtime senator, and Democratic state lawmaker James Talarico, 37.On the campaign trail, both contenders have been making similar clothing choices, wearing relaxed blazers and cowboy boots.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Despite political differences, Talarico, left, and Paxton have similar wardrobes"The necktie is dead on the campaign trail in both parties," says Ordway."The younger man dresses up to look serious, and the older man dresses down to look like one of the guys."Fashion critic Friedman notes that Talarico's handcrafted Lucchese cowboy boots "are a very deliberate choice that allows him to speak to all different kinds of constituencies in Texas"."Those boots mean something that is very deeply rooted in Texas semiology," Friedman says, referring to the study of signs and their interpretations. "Former US President George W Bush wore Lucchese cowboy boots, so suddenly you're crossing all sorts of party lines and tapping into all sorts of different electoral groups with your shoes."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Former US president George W Bush was a fan of cowboy bootsMeanwhile, Paxton's style of dress has come under fire on more than one front. It has drawn the disapproval of Trump who has urged voters to focus on his record because it "speaks a lot louder than the suit he's wearing that doesn't look so great".The Republican candidate has also been criticised by his opponent for wearing a pricey watch and polo shirt from the luxury hotel chain Four Seasons as a debate about the high cost of living dominates the midterms."The criticism around his apparent luxury watch and Four Seasons polo raises another style-branded question: casual clothes don't necessarily communicate an ordinary lifestyle," says Zee, a stylist and faculty associate at Arizona State University's Fashion Institute of Design and Merchandising."A five-star resort-branded polo can carry luxury associations just as clearly as a suit. "The watch's identity and value were unconfirmed, but the perception illustrates how an accessory can complicate a candidate's message," he explains.Image source, Facebook/KenPaxtonTXImage caption, Paxton's watch and Four Seasons polo shirt drew criticismPersonal uniformsA uniform, if it reads naturally, is an incredibly effective tool, says Friedman, and a great way to be recognised across the country.It's an approach adopted by Republican Senator and former congresswoman for Tennessee's 7th congressional district, Marsha Blackburn, who is running for governor of her state.Senator Blackburn is often seen in structured jackets and skirts, sometimes with patterns. Ordway remembers that Blackburn "was extremely polished" whenever he spotted her in Capitol Hill while working there as a legislative director for a former Indiana senator."I always saw pearls on her," he says. "Since she's a veteran politician I think how she dresses in relation to how voters see her was probably decided many, many years ago."Image source, BBC NewsImage caption, Marsha Blackburn has been wearing a consistent style for decades"Her looks tend to be fairly timeless - we could imagine GOP women wearing many of them any time in the last three decades," Kristian adds.Meanwhile, Michigan Democratic candidate for US Senate Abdul El-Sayed, who is in a highly competitive race against a Trump-backed former congressman, has adopted a consistent look of black V-neck T-shirt and blue jeans.The left-wing political outsider, whose campaign slogan is "money out of politics, money in your pocket", refers to his outfit choices as "minimal look, maximal politics". The effect, says Ordway, is reminiscent of a start-up entrepreneur, designed to appeal to an urban, working-class electorate.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Abdul El-Sayed calls his outfit "minimal look, maximal politics"It also removes much of the "ceremony of a political appearance", Zee says."The suggestion is that attention should go to what he is saying. But the plain T-shirt remains an image choice. Looking un-styled can still be a deliberate form of branding."Trump, master of the imageImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Trump's suit and red tie is instantly recognisableFriedman notes that the master of this look in the US at the moment is Trump. His instantly recognisable power suit and red tie, ever-present in film and reality TV, were cultivated even before he moved into the White House."[Trump] doesn't just have his own merch, but he's got his own outfit, and now he's got all his cabinet wearing the same outfit, and half the Senate is wearing his outfit, and it becomes like a Pavlovian signifier," Friedman says."If they're wearing a navy suit, red tie, and white shirt, you're like, 'oh, that's a Trump person,'" she says.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Vice-President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent wear similar looksWhatever the outcome of the elections for Trump and his party, Friedman expects to see more politicians effectively branding themselves with their clothing when the 2028 general election rolls in."What we see is that so much of politics now is fought over social media and over TV, and that places a premium on visual messaging that is only going to become more important."

schema.headline: 'The necktie is dead': How US midterm candidates are dressing for votes

title: Police watchdog to investigate Met over letter about Meghan's father
description: The UK police watchdog is to investigate the Metropolitan Police's handling of a letter containing allegations against Thomas Markle that was handed t
body: The UK police watchdog is to investigate the Metropolitan Police's handling of a letter containing allegations against Thomas Markle that was handed to his daughter, the Duchess of Sussex, in 2019.The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said it had decided an investigation was required into the force's "failure to pass on allegations of serious offending... to relevant overseas authorities at the time".The letter, written by Markle's first wife Roslyn Loveless, is believed to have contained claims about Meghan's father. He has strongly denied recent allegations that he had possessed images of child abuse, describing them as "sick lies".On Thursday the Met said it had voluntarily referred itself to the IOPC.The letter at the heart of the IOPC investigation was sent to the Met's royal protection team by Loveless, who divorced Thomas Markle in 1975 and died in 2024.The handwritten letter was then passed to Meghan in January 2019, with the duchess saying last week that it had "made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father".Meghan did not provide any details but said it had given her sufficient reason to not visit Thomas Markle and not allow him to meet his grandchildren, Archie and Lilibet.Scotland Yard said the letter contained claims about offending outside the UK and that it had been forwarded to "the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness".The IOPC will consider why the Met did not share the contents of the letter with other law enforcement agencies, in the UK or overseas.The policing watchdog also said it had decided a further matter, relating to an alleged data breach in which information was passed on to a third party, "should be returned to the force to be appropriately dealt with". No details were provided about the circumstances of the alleged breach.The Met said on Thursday that it intended to make further referrals to "relevant overseas law enforcement agencies", a process which it expected to be completed "in the coming days".The letter was forwarded by officers to the Sussexes' royal office rather than to Meghan personally, while there have been reports that the Met did not keep a copy of the letter and had to ask for one from the Sussexes.The watchdog will have to consider how the contents of the letter were treated by the force at the time.Noel Rasmussen, Thomas Markle's granddaughter and niece of the Duchess of Sussex, previously told the BBC she was "deeply troubled by the questions surrounding the Metropolitan Police's handling of the information it received". "If allegations of this seriousness were brought to the attention of authorities, it is reasonable to ask what steps were taken [and] why the information was not shared with other law enforcement agencies."Reports of the Met's handling of the letter emerged as Thomas Markle's son had told the police in the Philippines about material which was alleged to contain sexual images of children, which he had claimed to have found in possessions belonging to Meghan's father.Thomas Markle had been in the Philippines in December 2025, undergoing hospital treatment, when Meghan wrote to him to end all contact.Authorities in the Philippines have begun investigating the claims. Police there have obtained a warrant to examine devices seized from Markle's former home.Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old videotapes were handed to police by Meghan's half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, last week. However, officers in Cebu needed a court warrant before they can examine the items.Thomas Markle Sr has strongly denied all the allegations against him. He has been backed by his daughter Samantha, who has dismissed the claims against her father as "fake".
